title: Bitrunning
blurb: Plug into a netpod, raid a virtual domain, and haul the loot back out as real ore and gear.
text: Bitrunning is a dungeon crawl you do from inside your own ship. A quantum server generates a virtual domain, you lie down in a netpod and wake up in it as an avatar, and if you complete the domain's objective the ship's byteforge materialises the reward as physical cargo. It is the one expedition that does not need the ship to go anywhere, but it is not free, and it is not safe: the damage your avatar takes is passed straight through to the body lying in the pod. Getting a rig A working setup is four machines: a quantum server , a quantum console in a tile cardinally next to it, a byteforge within a few tiles, and at least one netpod . There are three ways to end up with them. Buy the Delta's Bitrunning Den. Delta's cafe slot has a fitout with three netpods, a server, a console and a byteforge already wired, and it adds a Bitrunner to the crew roster. See the ship purchase screen for what it costs. Print them. All four boards come out of the Bitrunning Technology node, which sits behind gaming and applied bluespace research. Any ship with a working R&D chain can build a den from scratch. Salvage one. The Nullstack Arcade, a rare ruin reachable only by rumour chart, is an overrun netpod parlour with its rig still bolted down and powered. It also has a netguardian and a Syndicate garrison standing on top of it. See Ruins & Points of Interest . Running a domain Pick a domain at the console. Each one lists a cost in points, a difficulty and a reward. The server starts the round with no points, so your first runs have to come from the free end of the list: Beach Bar, Gondola Asteroid, Grasslands Hunt, Breeze Bay. Completing domains earns points, which unlock the pricier ones. Choose an outfit and get in a pod. The netpod kits your avatar out; what your real body is wearing does not go with you. Find the encrypted cache. Every domain hides one. Some also hide a secondary objective (an encrypted curiosity) worth an extra reward. Carry it to the goal tile in the safehouse. That is the completion condition, not killing everything. The moment the cache lands on the goal, the byteforge back on the ship starts materialising a decrypted cache. Leave through a hololadder. Disconnecting cleanly means walking to an exit and taking it. There are only so many exits per domain, and each one you use is spent. Shutting a domain down puts the server into a cooldown of a couple of minutes, and everyone has to be disconnected before it will load a new one. What you get The decrypted cache pays in ore: iron and glass at every tier, then silver and titanium, then plasma, gold and uranium, and diamond and bluespace crystal on the richest domains. Higher-reward domains pay more of everything. Alongside the ore you get whatever loot that specific domain is written to drop, and a certificate graded on how fast you cleared it. Take a top grade on a domain of medium difficulty or worse and the crate also holds an experimental tech disk, once per domain, so the second clear will not pay it again. Rewards scale up with the number of runners connected, with a randomly-selected domain instead of a chosen one, and with the number of hostile intrusions the server threw at you on the way. Dying This is the part that catches people. Damage crosses over. Anything your avatar takes that is not stamina or oxygen damage is applied to your real body in the pod at the same time. Your body can be beaten to death by something that never touched it. A hard disconnect scrambles you. If the connection is severed rather than ended properly: your avatar dies, your body is knocked out, someone shuts the server down, the pod loses power or gets smashed: you come out with serious brain damage on top of everything else. Your body is a target. Attacking an occupied netpod is a real attack on the person inside. If the ship gets boarded while the crew is in VR, the runners are helpless. Leave the way you came. The hololadder is the clean exit and costs you nothing but the exit itself. Have someone awake A crew that puts everyone in a pod at once has nobody watching the ship, the console or the pods. Leave someone out. Boss domains Megafauna are rare in real space, but six virtual domains are built around one each: Domain Boss Ashen Inferno Ash drake Sanguine Excavation Blood-drunk miner Blood-Soaked Lair Bubblegum Celestial Trial Colossus Zealot Arena Hierophant Glacial Devourer Wendigo The objective is the same as any other domain: kill the boss, take the cache it was guarding, and get it to the goal tile. Each of these carries a briefing describing exactly what its boss does, attack patterns, what changes at half health, where the fight goes wrong. It is on the domain info action your avatar gets when you connect. Read it. Boss domains also do not pay for themselves. Every one of them costs more points to load than completing it returns, so a dive has to be funded by clearing the ordinary roster first. Threats A server that has been running domains all shift builds up threat, and a domain can boot with a malfunction in it: one of its own creatures taken over by a player from the dead, running as a temporary antagonist that is hunting you specifically. It makes the run harder, and every malfunction in a run raises the payout. There is no setting to turn it off.

title: The Grand Colosseum
blurb: A rare PvP venue that surfaces mid-round. Sign the ledger, fight strangers on the sand, and hope your gear ends up in your hands rather than the winner's.
text: The Grand Colosseum is a monumental fighting venue that surfaces on the overmap partway through a shift. It is the only place in the galaxy where crews can fight each other with no zone rules, no ship weapons and no consequences beyond what you walked in carrying. It is rare, one per round at most, and only if enough people are alive to fill a roster. Once it opens it stays open for the rest of the shift, running match after match. Getting there The venue surfaces no earlier than forty minutes into a shift and needs at least four players in the galaxy. It appears in the Contested band by preference (reachable from anywhere, not parked in the deep) and it announces itself galaxy-wide with its coordinates when it opens. Dock like you would at a trader outpost : your ship takes a hangar berth and you ride the alcove elevator up to the concourse. The building itself cannot be damaged. The doors cannot be hacked, welded or emagged, and there is no way onto the fighting floor except through the gates. Upstairs is an observation gallery behind a glass parapet, which is where you should be if you have not signed the ledger. Signing up Registration is not on a timer that runs by itself, anyone can walk to the concourse registration console and open the signup window, provided the venue is idle and the last match's cooldown has passed. Opening it broadcasts an invitation to the whole galaxy with the venue's position, so crews have time to fly in. The window runs for six minutes. Register at the console; you can withdraw again at any point before it closes. If fewer than two people have registered when the clock runs out, the whole thing fizzles and the venue resets. When the roster locks, the venue picks a game and an arena condition, announces both along with the prize pool, and starts a two-minute seating window. You do not have to walk anywhere: staying anywhere inside the venue is enough, and your berthed ship counts. The wardens teleport contestants into their cells or ready rooms when the seals close. Absentees are dropped from the roster and non-contestants are ejected from the staging areas. Then a ten-second countdown, and the gates open. You fight with what you brought Nobody is issued a kit. Whatever is in your hands and on your back when the gates open is what you have got, and whatever you leave on the sand belongs to the vault, not to you. The games The mode is chosen at random from those eligible for the roster size. Game Roster How it's won Free-for-All Deathmatch 2–12 Last fighter standing. Running out the clock pays nobody. Expiry is a draw. Team Deathmatch 4–16 Red vs blue, wipe the other team. Shipmates are kept on the same side. At the bell, the team with more fighters standing takes it. King of the Hill 2–8 Sixty cumulative seconds standing alone on the central dais. Sharing it with a rival accrues nothing for anybody. Eight-minute clock. Capture the Flag 4–16 Carry the enemy banner to your own plinth. Two captures wins. Banners are heavy, slow you down, and return to their plinth if left lying on the sand. Tournament 6–16 Rounds of elimination. Each round runs until its cut quota has fallen, then the wardens close the gates, carry the cut fighters out to spectate, sweep the arena and reseat the survivors. Last one standing takes a doubled prize pool. Arena conditions Every match rolls a condition alongside the mode: Clean Sands : no tricks, no beasts. Beast Interlude : the undercroft cages open. Beasts on the sand with you, and every kill adds to the purse. Scorching Sands : the floor braziers are stoked white-hot and the sand cooks whoever stands on it. Freezing Gale : glacier-cold air through the vents. Keep moving. Shifting Walls : the arena floor rebuilds itself mid-match. No lane stays safe. Raining Steel : weapon crates keep falling all match. Control the drops, control the match. Most modes also run a hazard scheduler during the fight, which rolls something every forty-five to ninety seconds: a weapon crate delivered by supply pod, a plus-shaped patch of sand that turns to lava for a few seconds, or destructible cover popping up out of the floor. All three are telegraphed by a warning marker on the tile a few seconds before they land. Watch the floor. The spoils vault When the match resolves, every gate opens, the winners are announced galaxy-wide, and the wardens sweep the arena. Everything loose on the fighting floor goes into the spoils vault: dropped items, the contents of weapon crates, and the corpses of the fallen. Living eliminated stragglers are carried off to the infirmary instead. Winners left standing on the sand are not touched. The prize pool goes into the vault at the same time, scaled to how many people fought and doubled for tournaments. Each winner gets a champion's extraction case holding their share of the pot: Roster Ship parts Credits Trade vouchers Up to 3 2 500 - 4–5 3 1,000 1 6–8 5 2,000 2 9+ 7 3,000 3 Ship parts lean heavily combat: this is the fighting venue. The champion's case is the useful part: it extracts in addition to your normal extraction case rather than competing with it, so a win is a genuine windfall for ship upgrades . For five minutes after the match the vault and its chamber answer only to the winners. They take first pick of the whole pile, their prizes and the loser's gear alike. When the window closes the vault unlocks for anybody who walks in, and the dead are laid out in the infirmary for their crews to collect. Losing is expensive If you die on the sand, your body and everything on it end up in the vault, and the people who killed you get first refusal on all of it for five minutes. Do not enter carrying anything you cannot afford to lose. Around the venue The Lanista's Rack is a gear stall on the concourse selling nine bespoke pieces of arena kit: gladiator armour, pit weapons and corner-man tools. The stock restocks after every settled match. The gear cannot be duplicated; the only source is the venue. The bookmaker's

title: Coming from /tg/station
blurb: A short list of everything a /tg/ veteran already knows that is wrong here, and everything that still works exactly the same.
text: If you have played /tg/station, most of your muscle memory transfers. Surgery, chemistry, atmospherics, botany, construction, combat, hacking. All of it is upstream code and all of it behaves the way you expect. What changed is the frame around it: there is no station, no shift, and no departments in the sense you are used to. This page is the diff. The round is a ship, not a shift There is no station and no arrivals shuttle. You start on a small crewed ship parked on the safe edge of a galaxy map, and that ship is the entire round for you. See The Overmap . You cannot call the emergency shuttle. Attempting it tells you so. There is no evac, no escape pods to fight over, and no round-end alert level theatre. A ship that wants out of the round can charge a bluespace jump at its own helm, which removes that ship and everyone on it from the round, that is as close as Voidcrew gets to escaping, and it is a per-crew decision, not a server-wide one. Because there is no station, there is also no permanent geography. Your medbay is a room on your ship that a random module roll gave you, and another crew's ship might not have one at all. No telecomms Radio does not route through machinery or z-levels here, so all the usual tricks are gone: no telecomms room to bomb, no signal degradation, no z-level dead zones, no relays to sabotage. Instead, every frequency except a few is scoped to a ship . Your headset binds to a ship the first time you use it aboard one (at job spawn for the headset you woke up in) and that binding is sticky. Take it onto a planet, a ruin or someone else's ship and your crew channel keeps working. A multitool re-tunes a headset to whatever ship it is currently standing in, which is also how you make a stolen headset useful. The one channel everyone shares is Wideband , prefix :w , a galaxy-wide hailing channel carried by every headset. Traders, pirates and events announce on it, and so can you. Counterplay lives at the item level now, EMPs, jammers and stealing headsets. See Comms . Antagonists Voidcrew does not build its rounds around an antagonist roster. Its own antagonist content is environmental and opt-in rather than assigned: pirates and NPC ships hunt you across the map, dynamic events go wrong on your ship, threats and elites guard the good loot, and vestige ruins (signals that surface one at a time as the round ages) hold patrons who will trade you a genuine ported antagonist ability for a bespoke trial. Heretic rites, changeling flesh, wizard spells and shadow walking are all things you can earn as a normal crewmember by doing something dangerous for something dead. See Vestige Ruins . The other source of antagonism is other players. Whether you are allowed to shoot them depends entirely on where you are standing, which is what the green, yellow and red zones exist to answer. Ship Combat covers doing it with the ship rather than a gun. Research and cargo Research is not a department you either have or do not have. Any ship with an autolathe (which is very nearly all of them) can print a Research & Development Kit for twenty iron and forty glass sheets, with no research needed, and that box contains the R&D console, protolathe, destructive analyzer, ship R&D server and (importantly) a circuit imprinter, which is the only machine that prints machine boards. Any hull can therefore bootstrap the whole suite. What a ship can build is a question of how far up the techweb it has climbed, not which rooms it launched with. Research points come from a survey scanner , a machine that converts power into points while parked somewhere new, rather than from standing around holding an experiment. There is also a radar research tree that extends how far your sensors reach and what they can identify. See The Overmap . Cargo is smaller and ship-shaped. Your ship has its own bank machine holding the ship's account, and a cargo console that orders against it; the supply shuttle flies out and docks alongside your ship rather than landing in a station bay. Most real money comes from traders and missions instead. See Money and Trade . Jobs and roles There is no fixed job roster. Each hull's theme defines its own crew. The same Goon-class might launch with Captain, Shaft Miner and Station Engineer, or Team Leader, Combat Engineer and Salvage Operative, depending on the theme it rolled. Modules can add jobs of their own. You therefore do not pick jobs in preferences; you pick categories (Command, Security, Engineering, Medical, Science, Cargo, Service, Assistant) at high, medium or low priority, and the game matches you to whatever that hull actually has. Each ship gets exactly one captain, contested between the players who wanted Command most. Job slots are not fixed either. The cryogenic oversight console aboard your ship adds and removes slots, up to six per job, on a two-minute cooldown, and the captain can shut off cryopod joining entirely. Access works off your ID as normal, but there is no station-wide access hierarchy to appeal to. If you cannot get into a room, the answer is the captain or a toolbox, not a bureaucracy. What has not changed Everything at personal scale. Medicine, surgery and cloning-adjacent care; chemistry and reagents; botany and hydroponics; atmospherics, pipes and canisters; power and the engine types; construction, deconstruction and wiring; guns, melee, wounds and combat; food, drinks and the bar; mechs, cyborgs and robotics; genetics and xenobiology; virology; the crafting menu; quirks and loadouts. If a page on this wiki does not exist for something, that is usually because it works the same and the /tg/station wiki already covers it. The one habit to unlearn On /tg/ the station is a fixed place you learn once. Here, the map, your ship's layout, your crew's jobs and half the machines aboard are rerolled every round. Read your own ship before you leave the dock.

title: Radio & Comms
blurb: Ship-scoped radio, the galaxy-wide Wideband channel, and holopad calls between ships.
text: There is no telecomms on Voidcrew. No relay to build, no stack to repair, no z-level to be on. Radio just works, everywhere, forever. What changed instead is who hears you : every ordinary channel is scoped to a single ship, so your crew chatter reaches your crew and nobody else. The one channel everyone in the galaxy shares is Wideband . Your ship's channel Press ; before a message to talk on your headset's main channel. On a station that would be the common channel; here it is your ship . Messages are tagged with the ship's name so you can tell at a glance which hull you are hearing. Department channels work the same way and are scoped the same way. Your engineering channel reaches the engineers on your ship, not the engineers on someone else's. Sticky binding Your headset binds to a ship, and that binding follows you off it. It is set when you spawn in, or the first time you use a radio while physically aboard a ship. Once bound it stays bound, walking onto a planet, into a ruin, or onto someone else's deck does not change it. This means: An away team on a planet still talks to the crew back on the ship. A boarding party keeps its own crew channel while standing inside the enemy hull, and can also overhear the local traffic of the ship it is standing in. A stolen headset stays bound to its old ship . Take one off a body and you are listening to their crew, not yours, until it is re-tuned. To re-tune a radio, use a multitool on it while aboard the ship you want it bound to. It rebinds to whatever hull it is currently sitting in. Check your headset before you trust it A headset picked up off the deck of a wreck, or handed to you by someone you just met, may still be transmitting to its original crew. Multitool it before you say anything sensitive on it. Wideband Wideband is the galaxy-wide hailing channel. Every headset carries it, no research or equipment is needed, and it reaches every radio in the galaxy regardless of distance or z-level. Speak on it by prefixing your message with :w or .w . Use it for the things that need to leave your hull: hailing a ship you can see, arranging a trade or a meeting, calling for help, warning other crews about something dangerous, or negotiating instead of shooting. It is also where a number of galaxy-wide events announce themselves, so expect traffic you did not ask for. Remember that a Wideband transmission tells everyone that you exist and that you are talking. It says nothing about where you are, but the people who want to find you are listening too. A few other frequencies are also unscoped and reach the whole galaxy rather than one ship, including the syndicate channel. If you are carrying a headset that has one, assume the wrong people can hear it. Ship-to-ship hails from the helm The helm console's Comms tab sends a short transmission from the ship itself. It reaches every vessel within your four-tile view ring (the same distance you can see) and lands on their helm as a logged message with a pulsing marker at your position. The trade-off is deliberate: hailing gives you away . A transmission identifies your ship on the receiver's chart exactly as if they had scanned you, so an anonymous blip that says hello stops being anonymous. Staying quiet is a valid tactic, and a pirate lurking on your tile has a reason not to greet you. See Piloting Your Ship . Holopad calls Holopads dial by site , not by area. Open one and the list shows: Rooms on your own ship, by area, like a station intercom. Every other ship in the galaxy, as one entry per ship: calling it rings every pad on that ship at once . Every trader outpost and player-founded outpost, the same way. Unregistered pads in ruins and wrecks, but only ones sharing your physical location. Calls are allowed galaxy-wide, matching Wideband. Answering projects the caller into the room as a hologram that can walk around, look, and talk. Two rules apply to calls between different ships: Nobody can force their way onto your pad. Cross-ship calls always ring and always have to be answered. Keycard authorisation cannot auto-connect a call from another vessel. Moving cuts the call. If either ship docks, undocks or jumps mid-call, the link drops and both pads announce that the carrier was lost. Calls within one ship are unaffected: both ends move together. The ringing pad also announces where the call is coming from, so you know which ship or outpost is on the line before you pick up. Pirate hails Hostile ships hail before they shoot. When one does, every holopad on your ship rings and the helm posts a priority alert. Answer it from the holopad interface: the incoming hail appears in the pad's call list alongside ordinary holocalls, labelled as a hostile vessel. Answering opens a negotiation with the pirate captain's hologram. You can pay them off, talk your way out, or stall. You have twenty seconds to answer, with a reminder at the halfway mark. Ignore it and they open fire. Lock weapons on them or shoot first, and the hail ends immediately and they engage. See Ship Combat . When comms go down Radios can be knocked out. An EMP silences everything it touches, radio jammers work the way they do on a station, and a communications blackout event kills every radio, intercom and holopad aboard one ship for about twenty seconds, including Wideband. Nothing needs repairing afterwards; the radios come back on their own. The warning you get is the blackout announcing itself over the very radios it is about, degrading into static mid-sentence. If a message cuts out like that, you have a few seconds before the ship goes quiet.

title: Cyberware
blurb: Chrome implants from the Chop Shop at the Undertow Exchange, neural capacity, the four tiers, the full catalog, and what an EMP does to a chromed body.
text: Cyberware ( chrome ) is a roster of implantable robotic organs sold at the Chop Shop , the neon-lit parlor off the Dregs cantina at the Undertow Exchange . Every piece does something no printed equipment does, from seeing in the dark to a deployable pair of hardlight blades, and every piece costs neural load against a fixed capacity, so a build is a budget rather than a shopping spree. Street chrome sells for credits; the good stuff wants vouchers . The Chop Shop Splice runs the parlor from behind counter glass. Click them for the shop, sorted into Street, Pro, Military and Legend tabs plus an ammunition shelf. Bought chrome lands in your hands as an organ, which does nothing until it is installed. Installation is the Chrome Cradle , the salvaged operating slab in the middle of the parlor, the only one in the galaxy. Drag yourself onto it and its console opens, showing your neural load, every piece of chrome within reach (installed, carried, or in the parts tray), and a projection of what any swap would cost and evict. Hit Install and the rig sedates you and does the work in seconds. Only you can ever order work on your own body, and only while conscious and unrestrained. Nobody can be strapped to the slab and carved for their chrome. Evicted and removed pieces wait in the parts tray, which anyone adjacent can eject. The Cradle also removes chrome in three seconds flat, and runs a tune-up for 200 credits that clears EMP scramble and repairs all your installed ware. If you carry the Chromatic Dermis ink suite, the Cradle's ink panel re-keys its color and pattern for free. Outside the parlor, ordinary organ-manipulation surgery at any operating table installs and removes chrome too, leg surgery exists for exactly this reason. Autosurgeons refuse the work entirely. Neural load Your body carries 20 points of chrome. Every installed piece sums its load against that, and the Cradle refuses any install that would take you over, though swapping within a ladder only costs the difference, since the piece being replaced comes out first. If you somehow end up over capacity anyway, everything browns out: every piece of chrome on your body goes offline until the load drops back under, and getting under is always as simple as pulling a piece out. Same-slot ware is mutually exclusive, one operating system, one dermal layer, one leg rig, one piece of hardware per arm, which makes most slots either a ladder (Shock Coils into Hopper Pistons, Dermal Mesh into Slabskin) or a straight choice (Cascade Lattice or Redline Core). Arm chrome always claims the whole arm: installing Mantis Blades evicts whatever that arm already carried. Chrome optics replace your natural eyes outright. The one piece that raises the ceiling is the Governor Delete, worth +6 capacity. Much of it shows. Plated arms, leg rigs, dermal weaves and spine lattices draw on your body under your clothes, and stacking enough chrome genuinely stops you looking human. The catalog Prices are Splice's, stock is limited per round, and load is the neural cost. "Pair" ware is sold as a cased set and installed one organ per arm. title: Drop Pods
blurb: A one-shot pod that puts you on a planet's surface, or through an enemy ship's hull.
text: An orbital drop pod is a reinforced closet with a drive in the back. It does two jobs. Fired from your ship it drops you onto the planet you are sitting over, so a crew does not have to land the whole hull to put people on the ground. Loaded into an assault pod tube it becomes a boarding weapon: the weapons officer throws it at another ship, and it cuts its own hole in their plating on the way in. Either way it is a one-way trip. Each pod fires once. Getting one Pods are printed, not crafted. They come off a protolathe once someone has researched Assault Pods , which sits under Shuttle Warfare Systems in the research tree alongside missiles and shields. Pod Materials Difference Orbital drop pod 15 iron, 5 titanium Opens itself when it lands Advanced orbital drop pod 15 iron, 15 titanium, 5 silver Tougher, insulated against outside heat and pressure, and stays sealed on arrival The advanced pod is what you want for a hostile world or a hot boarding action: it holds its own air and temperature, and it does not throw its hatch open the moment it stops moving. You choose when to be seen. Goon hulls have a pod aboard from the start. Dropping onto a planet Click the pod to bring up its control panel. Use it to open the doors, get in, and close them again. It will refuse to launch with the doors open. Then pick one of two launches: Random launch. Drops you on a random clear spot on the surface, never inside a cave. Directed launch. Puts you behind a targeting camera over the planet and lets you pick the tile. The targeting view marks each tile green or red. It refuses walls and unmined rock, chasms and anything else with no floor, the cordoned-off ground past the planet's edge, and any tile with a megafauna standing on it. Everything else is fair game. A pod crushes what is under it. Requirements, in short: The ship has to be sitting on a planet's tile, and that planet's surface has to be live. A planet that has been abandoned long enough to release its surface (see Planets ) will not take a pod until a ship docks there and brings it back up. The pod has to be aboard the ship, closed, and unused. Boarding another ship Boarding needs three things aboard: a pod, an assault pod tube , and a weapons system to fire it from. The tube is a machine built from a circuit board, and like every other ship weapon it has to be bolted against the outside of the hull, a tube buried in the middle of the ship has nothing to fire through. Multitool it onto the weapons system the same way you link a missile launcher; a tube that boots up next to a console links itself. Then: Someone climbs into the pod and seals the doors. Someone else drags the sealed pod onto the tube and loads it. That takes a few seconds, and once it is racked the pod's own launch controls are locked out: the weapons officer owns the launch from here. The weapons officer locks the target, enters the targeting camera, aims at a tile on the enemy hull, and hits Board . The pod crosses the gap like a missile, punches through the plating where it lands, and comes to rest inside, leaving a hole behind it that the rest of the boarding party can use. It will cut through a double-thickness hull, and no further: it is a doorway, not a tunnel. Armoured plating that refuses to break. Outpost hulls, mostly. Stops the pod on the outside face instead. Shields kill boarding parties A pod that hits a live shield detonates against it and everyone inside dies. Shields are why boarding is the last move of a fight, not the first: bring the shields down with lasers and missiles, then send people. The weapons system asks for confirmation before it launches into a shielded target, and the tactical plate shows the target's shield pool the whole time. The same rules that stop you shooting at people apply to boarding them, you cannot launch a pod in patrolled green space, and a tube reports itself safed when the zone forbids it. Getting home The pod is a one-shot. It stays where it lands and makes a serviceable shelter, but it will not fly again. Plan the trip back before you launch: Link a quantum pad. Buffer a quantum pad with a multitool and use the multitool on the pod before launching. Once the pod is down, its Teleport button sends everything inside it (or, if the doors are open, everything on its tile) to that pad. It works exactly once, and the pad has to be powered and intact when you press it. Or have the ship collect you. The alternative is the ship coming to you and the pod crew walking to it. That costs nothing but time, and it is the usual answer when the whole crew went down together. One pod, one trip A pod that has fired cannot be re-armed and the teleport cannot be used twice. Two people who both want a ride home need either two pods or a plan. See Planets for what is waiting on the surface, Piloting for getting the ship into orbit over one, and Ship Combat for the fight that comes before a boarding action.

title: Random Events
blurb: Events here pick one ship and happen to that ship. Which ship, and how badly, depends on your crew size, your hull and the zone you're parked in.
text: On a station, a random event hits the station. Here there is no station, so every event picks one crewed ship and confines itself to that ship's decks. A meteor wave that lands on somebody else is genuinely somebody else's problem. The ship next to them, the ruin they were docked at and the outpost down the road are all structurally untouchable by it. This also means events are not shared misery. When the deck starts shaking, it is shaking for you and nobody is coming to help. How targets get picked Roughly every three to eight minutes, one event fires somewhere in the galaxy. With several crewed ships flying, that works out to one event per ship far less often than it sounds. Selection is not uniform. Every ship in play is checked against the event's own requirements, and the survivors are weighted by how many crew are aboard . A ship with six people on it is six times as likely to be picked as a ship with one. After a ship is hit it gets a four-minute reprieve before ambient events will consider it again. The requirements are where most of the safety lives: Zone. Most dangerous events refuse to fire outside the Contested and Lawless bands. A handful: the meteor storm, the immovable rod, pyroclastic and vortex anomalies, the advanced disease: are Lawless-only. See the overmap for the bands. Hull size. Destructive events set a minimum ship size. A three-tile hull with no airlock and no medbay does not get a vortex anomaly or a portal storm dropped on it, because that is not an event, it is the end of the round for everyone aboard. Crew count. Some events need two or three people aboard to make any sense. Flying. The meteor family and the carp migration only fire at ships out on the overmap. A landed ship shares its ground with whatever it landed on, and cratering a ruin because one crew rolled a meteor wave is not the intent. Safe harbour. Ships docked at a trader outpost are skipped entirely. Some events also have an earliest-start time, so the nastier material only turns up well into a shift. What you'll actually see A sample of the roster, roughly from routine to serious: Event What happens Ventilation clog Harmless mobs climb out of a vent. Mostly a mess. Ship camera failure A chunk of your camera network goes dark. Micrometeoroid shower Grit and sand pit the hull. Might break a window. Ship grid check Every APC aboard shuts off until somebody reboots them by hand. Gravity generator failure The deck loses gravity for a few minutes. Communications blackout Every radio aboard cuts out for a while. Scrubber overflow The scrubbers vomit foam through the ship. Three severities. Space vines Kudzu takes root and starts eating the ship. Radiation leak A machine starts leaking until somebody repairs it. Stray cargo pod A pod containing a random supply crate lands aboard. Free loot. Ship grey tide Airlocks in one or two areas bolt open. Meteor shower / storm Waves of rock through the hull. The storm opens compartments. Immovable rod A rod passes clean through the ship. Portal storm Syndicate shocktroops pour out of portals on your deck. There are anomalies too (gravitational, bluespace, dimensional, hallucination, pyroclastic, vortex) and a long tail of small stuff: mice, a cow that tells you wise things, a random animal becoming sentient, spontaneous brain trauma, a fake virus, a market crash that raises vending prices sector-wide. Not everything is bad. The stray cargo pod, at least, is a gift. Reducing your exposure Dock at a trader outpost. Ships in a safe harbour are removed from the target pool outright. If you need to do repairs, do them there. Stay in the Neutral Zone. It is not immunity (the harmless events fire anywhere) but the ones that open your hull mostly won't touch you there. Fly a small ship, or accept the consequences of a big one. Size gates work both ways: a big hull is what makes the serious events eligible against you. Land. The meteor family and the carp migration require you to be out flying. Don't stack your whole crew on one hull. The weighting is per-ship crew count, so the flagship with everyone aboard is the ship the galaxy keeps picking on. None of this makes you safe. Have a welder, spare plating, an extinguisher and a hardsuit somewhere everyone can reach. Contested caches Separate from the event roster, and worth flying for. Thirty minutes into a shift a bonded courier drop platform surfaces in Contested or Lawless space, and the whole sector is told about it: a broadcast on every open channel, a priority announcement, and a waypoint pushed to every ship's helm. There is no mystery here, the announcement names the location and states plainly that the vault's escrow seals disengage in ten minutes . That ten minutes is the point. Every crew in the galaxy heard the same message and knows every other crew heard it too. What happens in that window is up to you: get there first and hold the platform, arrive late and take it off whoever did, or stay away. When the clock runs out the vault unseals and anyone alive can start forcing it open by hand, a thirty-second job that any hit interrupts. First crew to finish it gets the contents: a crate of five ship parts, weighted heavily toward combat parts, plus an extraction case to carry them in. The galaxy is then told the cache has been claimed. Claiming it is not keeping it The prize is a physical crate. It still has to be cased, carried back to your ship and extracted, and everyone in the sector was just told who has it. The dangerous part of a contested cache is usually the flight home. The vault itself is indestructible (you cannot skip the window with a welder or a bomb) and the platform retires itself twenty minutes after the claim, or thirty minutes after the unseal if nobody ever showed up. Two of these surface per round at most, the second roughly fifty minutes after the first. Ship parts are the currency of hull and module upgrades , which is why a cache is worth a fight.

title: Fuel & Gas
blurb: Where thruster fuel comes from, nebula scooping, plasma sublimation, and selling exotic gas to traders.
text: Most ships fly on burnt gas, and gas costs money. A crew that buys every canister off a trader will spend a large fraction of its income on getting anywhere. There are two ways to stop doing that: scoop your fuel out of a nebula, or bake it out of plasma you mined. Both are machines you build once and run forever, and the second-order effect is that the rarer gases become something you sell rather than burn. How ships burn fuel Fuelled thrusters do not hold their own fuel. Each one draws from an engine heater parked directly behind it and facing the same way. The heater is the tank; the thruster is the nozzle. For how these fit into the rest of the hull. See Ship Systems . A heater feeds from one of two sources, toggled by alt-clicking it: Tank mode , where it drinks from a gas tank you slotted into it. Simple, portable, and small. Pipe mode , where it drinks from whatever pipe network it is wrenched onto. This is the mode that matters, because it is what lets a fuel machine somewhere else on the ship keep the engines topped up automatically. The two common fuelled thrusters differ a lot in appetite. A plasma thruster burns plasma specifically, and is the efficient one. An expulsion thruster burns literally any gas and is far less efficient per mole. It is what you install when you have more gas than sense, or when the only thing you can scoop is nitrogen. Heavier ships burn proportionally more per burn, so a big hull with a small fuel supply is a bad combination. See Piloting for how burns work at the helm. Nebulas Nebulas are common features on the overmap , and in Voidcrew every one of them carries a specific gas . Which gas depends on how deep the nebula is: the safe outer ring holds plasma, nitrogen and water vapour; the contested band adds tritium and miasma; and the lawless deep is where hypernoblium, pluoxium and nitrium pool. Your helm names each nebula after its gas and tints it on the chart, so you can pick a tritium cloud out of a bank of them without flying into each one. Nebulas also block sensors . Sitting inside one lets you engage nebula concealment and disappear off other crews' contact lists, which makes them the standard place to hide from a ship that is hunting you. The ram scoop A nebula ram scoop is an external intake you build on your hull and wrench onto a pipe network. It harvests only when three things are true at once: the intake is open, your ship is inside a nebula , and your ship is holding still . Click it to open or close the intake. Harvested gas feeds straight into the connected pipes. Run those pipes to an engine heater in pipe mode and your engines refuel themselves; run them to a connector port instead and you can fill canisters and tanks to sell or carry. Scoop rate depends on the gas. The common fuels come in fast; the valuable ones come in slowly on top of only existing in dangerous space. Better micro-lasers in the scoop multiply the rate, a full set of top-tier lasers roughly quadruples it. Scooping is loud Running the scoop cancels nebula concealment and rips away any concealment you already had , and keeps you visible for ten seconds after the last harvest tick. You cannot refuel and hide at the same time. Every crew in the galaxy knows the fuel stop is also the ambush spot. Close the intake before you try to hide. The sublimation chamber The plasma sublimation chamber is the other half of the loop, for crews who mine rather than fly around looking for clouds. Feed it raw plasma sheets by hand (the hopper holds fifty) and it bakes each sheet down into 30 moles of clean plasma gas, trickled into whatever pipe network it is wrenched onto. Alt-click empties the hopper back into sheets if you change your mind. Micro-lasers set the output rate here too. Since planets and asteroids hand out plasma ore fairly freely, a mining crew with a sublimator effectively never buys fuel again. Both machines are unlocked by the same early research node as the engine heater, so any ship that can research at all can print both boards. Waystation Halcyon also sells the ram scoop board over the counter for 600 credits, which is the route for crews with no research bay. Buying fuel If you would rather just buy it, both the general waystation and the outfitter depot keep fuel and breathing gas on the shelf: Item Waystation Halcyon Quartermain Depot Full plasma canister 1800 cr 1100 cr Welding fuel tank 400 cr 400 cr Full oxygen tank 150 cr 120 cr Nebula ram scoop board 600 cr - Quartermain is cheaper on plasma because it sits further out; Halcyon's markup is the haul to the safe ring. Selling gas Exotic gas is worth real money, and there is exactly one buyer: Vex at the Undertow Exchange , in the lawless deep. Vex buys gas by the tank . Fill a tank off your scooped pipe network at a connector port, carry it to the counter, and the tank goes with the sale. Gas Pays Minimum in one tank Hypernoblium 1200 cr 200 mol Pluoxium 300 cr 200 mol Nitrium 300 cr 200 mol All three only pool in deep-band nebulas, and all three scoop slowly, so the payout is gated by how long you are willing to sit still in the most dangerous space in the galaxy with your position broadcast. See Trader Outposts for getting to Vex. Gas Harvest contracts on your ship's mission board are the other sink. Each asks for a tank holding a required quantity of one specific gas, and the board only ever asks for a gas that a nebula somewhere in this round's galaxy actually carries. The common gases pay 700–1200 credits for 600–900 moles; tritium pays 1500–2200 and a voucher; the deep-band exotics pay 2000–3200 and a voucher for as little as 150 moles. Any tank works, and the contract keeps the tank. See Missions . Practical advice for a new crew Build the scoop early. It is one board, it costs less than three canisters, and it removes your largest recurring expense. Put the heater in pipe mode. A heater on a tank has to be hand-fed. A heater on the pipe network refuels itself off the scoop or sublimator while

title: Glossary
blurb: Every Voidcrew-specific word you will hear on the radio in your first hour, defined in one line each.
text: Voidcrew adds a vocabulary that /tg/station does not have, and most of it turns up on the radio before anyone explains it. This page is the lookup table. Anything not listed here almost certainly means the same thing it means on /tg/station . The map Term Meaning Overmap The galaxy map, a 51-by-51 grid of tiles with a star at the centre, on which your whole ship is one icon. See The Overmap . Zone One of three static concentric rings on the overmap that decide what crews may do to each other. Named on the helm readout and colour-tinted on the map. Neutral Zone (green) The outer ring. Ship weapons are disabled and nobody can interdict you. Every ship starts here. Traders call it the neutral ring. Contested Zone (yellow) The middle ring. Ship weapons are still disabled, but you can be interdicted and boarded. Traders call it the contested lanes. Lawless Zone (red) The inner ring, nearest the star. Everything is permitted, and the ore and loot are the best in the galaxy. Traders call it the lawless deep. Contact Anything drawn on the helm's navigation chart: a planet, ruin, storm, outpost or vessel. Active scan A one-minute-cooldown sensor sweep that charts contacts beyond visual range onto your navigation list. Range grows with radar research. Star chart A one-use slate bought from traders that charts every contact in one whole zone at once, including storms your own sensors cannot detect. Rumor chart Bought intel naming one rare ruin. Decrypting it at the helm spawns that ruin and marks it gold on the map. Dread signal A vestige ruin's overmap contact, marked in red and named for the patron inside (e.g. "Sister Havel", "the Weaver"). They surface one at a time as the round ages. Nebula A harmless overmap cloud of one specific gas. A ram scoop harvests it, and it is the only place a ship can hide. See Gas Economy . Asteroid storm A landable rock field. Flying through one damages your hull; docking with it lets you mine it. See Mining . Encounter Any interior the game builds on demand when you dock: a planet surface, a ruin, an asteroid field, or a patch of empty space. Your ship Term Meaning Hull A ship class: the base map, its rooms and its docking port. See Ship Catalog . Theme A whole-ship variant of a hull: a different look, layout and crew roster on the same frame. One Goon-class can launch as NT Standard or as a Syndicate Cutter. Module A room that drops into one of a hull's upgrade slots, adding equipment and sometimes an extra job. See Ship Upgrades . Upgrade slot A marked pocket in a hull that exactly one module loads into. Every slot always gets something. Helm The console that flies the ship, draws the navigation chart, runs scans and docks. See Piloting . Integrity Your ship's health, which is literally how much of it is still standing. Every floor counts one, walls two, reinforced walls three. Rebuilding repairs it. Ship channel Your crew's radio. Every frequency except a few is scoped to one ship, and your headset stays bound to it even off the ship. See Comms . Wideband The galaxy-wide hailing channel, prefix :w , carried by every headset. Traders, pirates and events all announce on it. Cryogenic oversight console Manages job slots (up to six per job, two-minute cooldown) and whether latejoiners may wake up aboard. Bank machine Holds the ship's shared account. Cargo and traders draw on it. See Money and Trade . Mission board The console that offers and tracks contracts. See Missions . Mission pad The pad that sits beside the board. Put mission items on it to hand them in, and rewards appear on it. Techweb Your ship's research tree. It lives on the source code disk inside your own R&D server, starts empty, and is not shared with any other crew. See Research . Research points The currency of the techweb, earned by experiments, surveys and salvaged documents rather than handed out over time. See Research . Research notes A physical document with a point value printed on it. Press it against an R&D console to bank the points, or sell it to cargo for half a credit per point. Survey scanner A machine that turns power into research points while parked somewhere new. See Research . Orbital survey console The console that surveys whatever your ship is orbiting, paying points and credits and recording the object against research that requires it. Transporter A pad-and-console pair that beams people and cargo between the ship and a surface. See Transporters . Transponder The palm-sized beacon you carry that pairs to one transporter pad, letting the ship see you and pull you home. Drop pod A one-shot pod that drops you onto whatever the ship is parked over, or gets fired through an enemy hull out of an assault pod tube. See Drop Pods . Abandoned ship A ship whose crew has all died or left. It stops accepting joiners until somebody claims it at its helm. Money and progression Term Meaning Ship parts Physical items in four classes (combat, science, trade and misc) that persist between rounds and unlock hulls, themes and modules. Extraction case The secure case parts must be sitting in, on your person, for them to survive the round. Request one with the Request Extraction Case verb. Only the first standard case counts. Voucher A trade voucher: a physical chit earned from dangerous work, never bought with credits, and spent at any trader for restricted goods. Being an item, it can be stolen off you. Chrome Cyberware, implantable robotic organs sold at the Chop Shop on the Undertow Exchange. See Cyberware . Neural load What each piece of chrome costs against your 20-point capacity. Going over capacity browns every piece out at once. Trader outpost One of three permanent markets, one per zone: general store in green, outfitter in yellow, black market in red. Turrets shoot people who keep starting fights. See Trader Outposts . Player outpost A base a crew plants for itself using an outpost deed. See Player Outposts .
