title: Mining & Salvage
blurb: Fly somewhere with rock in it, dig, haul the ore home, turn it into sheets or credits.
text: There is no station mining outpost here and no shuttle that goes to it. Ore comes from places you fly to: planet surfaces, asteroid storms, and the ruins in between. The whole loop is fly out, dig, haul it back aboard, and convert it, into material sheets at the ship's own redemption machine, or into money at a trader's counter. Everything about swinging a pickaxe works the way it does on /tg/; what follows is only what Voidcrew does differently. Where the rock is Planet surfaces. Every planet has rock pockets carved into its terrain with mineral walls inside them. This is the most available digging there is, and it comes with everything else a planet has. See Planets . Volcanic and apocalyptic crust also hides raw telecrystal, and frozen permafrost hides glacial cores. Asteroid storms. These are the dedicated mining sites. They appear on the chart as storm hazards in three severities, and there are always at least three somewhere in the galaxy. Fly onto one and press Dock. The button reads "(mining anchorage)", and you are put inside the field, a scatter of rock blobs with hard vacuum between them. Storm Ore Guarded cache Minor Iron, plasma, silver, titanium, a little gold Occasionally Moderate The above plus uranium, diamond and bluespace in the tail Often Major Same list, far richer, and the densest rock of the three Usually, and often the rare kind The toll is paid on the way in: crossing a storm tile throws a rock at your hull, and the worse the storm, the bigger the rock. Every field also carries roaming packs of hostiles, and any cache in it is guarded. Ruins. Salvage counts. Ruin interiors hold sheets, machines you can unbolt and carry, and loot caches. See Ruins & Points of Interest . Ore vents Volcanic and frozen worlds put ore vents out in their terrain. A vent is a permanent ore supply, but it has to be taken first: Hit it with a mining scanner to survey it. That tells you which minerals it carries and pays mining points to your ID. Scan it a second time to start the excavation. A node drone attaches itself to the vent and the ground opens up: goliaths, legions, watchers, lobstrosities, brimdemons and bileworms come out and go for the drone. Keep it alive and in place until the wave ends. Win, and the vent is tapped for the rest of the round. It produces boulders; break them with a pickaxe to get the ore out. Lose the drone and the vent seals up. You can try again. Bring the scanner A vent cannot be surveyed or tapped without a mining scanner, and it will not tell you what is inside until it is surveyed. Waystation Halcyon sells one. Tendrils Corrupted tendrils grow on volcanic worlds. They are nests, not vents: they pour out monsters until killed. When one dies the ground collapses, and for about five seconds anyone standing there can pull one crate out of it by hand. One crate per person, then the tile becomes a chasm. The contents are the good stuff. This is where berserker armour, gauntlets, an eye of god and the kinetic accelerator modkit discs come from. Getting it home Ore goes back to the ship in an ore box or a bag; the ship converts it. Ore redemption machine. Feed it ore, get material sheets that the ship's lathes can spend. Unlike the station version, ship machines have no ID lock: anyone aboard can use one. How to load it. There is no insert button. The machine watches one adjacent tile (marked with a blue arrow, by default the one directly behind it) and swallows anything that lands there. Drop loose ore on that tile, or set a whole ore box down on it and the entire contents go in at once. Sheets come out the opposite side, marked in red. If the panel is open you can alt-click to rotate which sides do what. Which hulls have one. Most do, and on modular hulls it belongs to a specific fitout: Goon's Prospector Bay (the default in that slot), Delta's Mining Bay, Kilo's Ore Refinery, Phalanx's Muster Deck. The alternatives in those same slots deliberately trade the redemption machine away for salvage or freight gear, so check the module before you buy it. If your ship has no redemption machine A welder will smelt ore straight into sheets, one unit of welder fuel per chunk: iron ore into iron, sand into glass, and most other ores into their metal. Plasma is the exception. A welder cannot get hot enough for it, so plasma ore is the one thing you cannot process without a machine. That matters more than it sounds, because plasma sheets are what portable generators burn: a ship with no redemption machine can mine plasma all day and still run out of fuel. Three ways out of that, cheapest first: Buy sheets. The general store's fuel counter stocks solid plasma in twenties. Raw plasma ore is also on the shelf and works out cheaper per sheet, but only buy that if you have a machine to run it through. Sell the ore. Traders take plasma ore on their supply contracts, so it is never worthless even if you cannot use it. Build a redemption machine. Any ship with an autolathe can get there. The autolathe prints a Research & Development Kit from the start with no research needed: 20 iron and 40 glass sheets, both of which a welder can make from ore you dug yourself. That box holds the circuit imprinter, which is the only machine that prints circuit boards. From there, Mining Technology is one cheap step off a free starting node, and it unlocks the redemption machine board. It is a long detour, but it is the permanent fix. - Mining points ride on your ID, and vent work pays them out directly: you are credited for surveying a vent and again for tapping it. A mining equipment order console spends them, and orders through it are delivered immediately by pod where you stand rather than riding a shuttle. Only a few hulls carry one: Delta's Mining Bay is the one you can buy. Selling it Traders at outposts run a wanted ledger: a list of things they are buying this round, with a limited appetite for each. Sell there and payment lands on your ID, or in your hand for vouchers. Goods Sold at Pay

title: Missions
blurb: The contract board every ship carries, the mission pad, what the contracts ask for, and what they pay.
text: Missions are the reliable way to make money in Voidcrew. Every standard hull carries a mission board that posts fresh contracts all round, and a mission pad next to it where you hand things in and rewards appear. Contracts pay credits into the ship account and, on the dangerous ones, trade vouchers into your hand. The board and the pad The mission board is a console. It links itself to any mission pad within a few tiles, and the two work as a unit: the board is where you accept, track, and turn in, and the pad is where physical objects change hands. The board keeps five offers posted at a time and tops itself back up as you take them. An offer nobody accepts rotates off after 20 minutes and is replaced. A refresh button wipes all five and deals a new hand, on a 5-minute cooldown. Use it when the board has nothing your crew can do, not to fish for the top-paying contract. Your ship can run three missions at once . Each has its own clock, usually 30 minutes, longer on the planet-side contracts. Accepting a contract does three things: it starts the timer, it drops a waypoint on the helm chart so the pilot can find the target, and for some contracts it dispenses equipment onto your mission pad. Tapping a handheld GPS unit on the board uploads the objective beacons of every active mission to that unit, which is how you find a small object inside a large ruin. Contracts with more than one step show a checklist on the board, and only one step is live at a time. The board tells you which. Turning in Contracts finish one of two ways. If there is nothing to hand over (exploration, surveying, a kill sweep) the turn-in button goes live once the objectives are satisfied. If the contract wants something physical, put it on the pad first , then pick it from the item list on the board and turn in. Rewards arrive in two places: credits go straight into the ship's bank account, while vouchers and item rewards materialise on the pad. Missions fail on the clock A contract that times out is a failure, and the ship is told about it. If it is going badly, abandon it from the board instead. Abandoning costs nothing and frees the slot. Some contracts also fail if the thing they are about is destroyed. Recovery-family contracts will quietly re-pick a target twice before giving up; contracts built around one specific creature, beacon, or batch just void. Pay and zones Every contract that points somewhere on the overmap is priced by the zone band its target sits in. Deeper is worth more: a contract in the contested middle band pays roughly 1.7× the outer-ring rate, and one in the lawless deep pays about 2.6×. Contracts in the deep also add an extra trade voucher on top of whatever they already paid. The board labels each offer Easy, Medium, or Hard, and that label is just the zone band restated. A "hard" contract is not a harder puzzle. It is the same job somewhere that will shoot at you. The contract types Contract What it asks Delivery Contract Bring a listed quantity of ore, sheets, or crystals to the pad. No travel required if you already have the goods. Exploration Contract Fly the ship to marked coordinates, then come home and collect. Survey Contract Scan a number of celestial objects (nebulas, asteroid fields, planets, stars, storms) with the orbital survey console. Recovery Contract Retrieve a named object from inside a space ruin and carry it back to the pad. Kill Contract Hunt down a named pirate captain holed up in a ruin and bring back their identification tag. Harder targets keep bodyguards. Survey Contract (pylons) Calibrate three survey pylons inside a ruin, one at a time. Each calibration is loud and draws a wave of defenders. The last pylon prints the core you carry home. Extraction Contract Unbolt a fixed piece of cargo inside a ruin. Wrenching it loose takes time and trips an alarm that answers in two waves. Rescue Contract A survivor is alive inside a wreck. Get them out and back to the pad breathing. The fee doubles if they are unharmed. Suppression Sweep Confirm a number of pirate kills anywhere in the contested band or deeper. No item turn-in; it settles at the board. Gas Harvest Contract Deliver a tank holding a required quantity of a specific gas. See Fuel & Gas . Field Expedition A probe went down on a planet. Find the wreck, pull its core, and be ready for whatever lifting it wakes up. Big Game Hunt Stake a supplied lure on a planet surface, kill the apex predator it draws out, and carry back a trophy. Live Capture Track a survey-marked animal on a planet, wear it down without killing it, and seal it in the supplied crate. It has to arrive alive. Poacher Bust Raid an illegal hunting camp on a planet, wipe the squad, and recover their tagged evidence cache. Prospect Stake Fly to marked coordinates in the contested band or deeper, deploy the supplied claim beacon aboard your ship, and keep it intact for eight minutes while holding station. The filing goes out on Wideband, so the whole sector knows. Top of the pay curve, and the deep-band version sometimes pays a crate of ship parts instead of vouchers. Not every type is available at once. Several are capped so the galaxy only ever has one or two running, and the planet contracts only appear when a planet of the right kind is actually in this round's sector. Read the description before you accept Each offer's text names its coordinates, its zone band, its beacon tag, and whether it dispenses equipment. The planet contracts in particular hand you a lure, a crate, or a claim kit at accept, if you launch without collecting it off the pad, you have wasted the run. Bounties and broadcasts The board carries three things besides contracts. Pirate bounties are competitive: a named pirate captain is posted galaxy-wide, several crews can hunt the same one, and it goes to whoever kills them and puts their ship key on the mission pad. Paying a fee out of the ship account tracks the target on your chart, deducted from the reward. Player bounties let you

title: Money & Trade
blurb: Credits, trade vouchers, the ship bank, the cargo console, and the schematics that unlock new gear.
text: Voidcrew has no station budget and no paychecks. Every credit your crew spends is one you earned by selling something, finishing a contract, or taking it off somebody else. There are two in-round currencies. Credits, which live in your ship's shared bank account, and trade vouchers, which are physical chits you carry, and they buy different things on purpose. The two currencies Credits are the everyday money. They sit in one bank account shared by the whole crew: when you spawn, your ID is bound to the ship's account rather than a personal one, so anything anyone earns goes into the same pot and anything anyone spends comes out of it. The account starts empty. Credits pay for cargo orders, most trader stock, neural imprint fees, outpost deeds, and bounties you post yourself. Trade vouchers are tamper-sealed chits that stack in your pocket like cash. They cannot be bought with credits, ever. You earn them by finishing dangerous contracts and by selling traders loot that can't be manufactured aboard a ship. Planet minerals, fauna harvests, ruin finds, deep-band gases. Any trader outpost honours them. Being a physical item, they can also be dropped, stolen and demanded as pirate tribute, so carrying a large stack into the deep is a real decision. What vouchers are for Vouchers buy the tier of gear no shop will sell for money: weapon schematics, syndicate MODsuit hardware, ship shield and interdiction boards, military-grade cyberware , top-tier exploit software , and the charts that reveal rare ruins. If you want any of that, you have to go somewhere dangerous. There is also an out-of-round currency, ship parts , extracted at the end of a round and spent between rounds on new hulls and modules. See Ship Upgrades ; it has nothing to do with the credits in your bank. The ship bank Every standard hull carries a bank machine among its ship systems . It displays the account balance and is what the cargo console draws money from. Examining it tells you which account it is connected to. If the machine ever loses its link (you built a new one, or the ship changed hands) swipe an ID card on it to connect that card's account. A multitool copies the machine into its buffer so you can point a cargo console at it. The bank machine is also where physical money turns into spendable credits. Loose cash and holochips looted out of a ruin do nothing sitting in your bag; feed them to the machine and the value lands in the ship's account. It refuses cash while it has no account connected, so nobody wastes a holochip on an unlinked machine. Your own ID is what pays at trader counters, at the neural imprinter, and for outpost broadcasts. If your ID has no account on it, those machines will refuse you. The cargo console The cargo console is how you buy supply crates and bulk-sell salvage. It orders from the standard supply catalogue, and it only works when your ship is docked in empty space and holding still . You cannot call cargo while flying, at a planet, or at an outpost. The flow: Add packs to the cart. The total is checked against the ship account. Hit send. A cargo shuttle arrives after about 30 seconds and docks alongside your ship. Your order materialises in its bay and a requisition form prints at the console. Carry the crates aboard. Load anything you want to sell into the bay. Hit send again. The shuttle takes 5 seconds to leave, then everything left in its bay is sold and the proceeds land in the ship account. The console announces what sold and for how much, and keeps a scrollable transaction history. Clear the shuttle before you send it The shuttle refuses to depart with a living creature aboard, and everything else left in the bay is sold. Do not leave your toolbox on the floor. Export values are roughly a quarter of what the same item costs to buy, so you cannot make money by cycling crates. Cargo turns salvage, ore and unwanted loot into credits; it is not an arbitrage machine. Two extras: coupons found in loot slot into the console for a discount on a matching pack, and supply companies occasionally offer a loan , free credits now in exchange for a crate of their goods riding along on the next delivery. Selling to traders The cargo console is not the only buyer. Every trader outpost keeps a wanted ledger : a short list of things that trader is buying this round, with a fixed payout each. See Trader Outposts for where to find them. Selling at a counter differs from cargo in three ways: The trader takes goods from anywhere on you: hands first, then bags and pockets. Anything you are wearing is skipped, so you cannot accidentally sell the suit off your back. Credit payouts go to your ID's account. Voucher payouts appear in your hand. Each ledger entry has limited demand for the round. Once the trader has bought all they want, that line closes until a supply convoy comes through. Sample lines: Barnaby at the waystation pays 300 credits per five gold ore, 500 per two diamonds, 150 for any fresh fish. Roux at the waystation diner pays 60 per home-cooked meal, 120 per hand-made pie and 180 per whole cake, real cooking only, never vending-machine food or her own plates. Sarge at the depot pays 250 per two goliath hide plates, 400 per three glacial cores. Vex at the black market is the only trader who pays in vouchers, one per five raw telecrystals, one per legion core, two per set of syndicate documents. Traders also buy gas by the tank; see Fuel & Gas . Blueprints and the imprinter Some weapons cannot be researched, bought assembled, or printed. They exist only as schematics : rolled-up paper you find in ruin loot or buy from a trader. While you are carrying a schematic anywhere on your person, its recipe appears in your ordinary crafting menu. No workbench is involved; you can build it wherever you are standing. Gun recipes still consume a machined weapon component (printed at a protolathe behind its research node) plus a firing pin, so the schematic is the permission, not the whole cost. Six schemati

title: New Player Guide
blurb: Your first shift. How you get a ship and a crew, what is already aboard, and what to do with all of it.
text: There is no station in Voidcrew. When the round starts you are dropped onto a small ship with a handful of other players, somewhere on the safe edge of a galaxy map called the overmap , and everything you do that round happens on that ship or somewhere you flew it to. This page covers your first hour. Joining a round Ready up in the lobby like normal. When the round starts, the server counts how many people readied and builds a fleet to match: one hull per six ready players, up to four hulls. Everyone who readied is dealt out evenly across those hulls, so a full server is several separate crews flying separate ships, not one big crew. Each hull is rolled at random: a hull class, one of that class's themes, and a random module in every one of its upgrade slots. Nobody chooses this and nobody pays for it, so the ship you wake up on is a surprise every round, and while the pool lasts no two hulls in the fleet are the same class. See Ship Catalog for the hulls and Ship Upgrades for what themes and modules change. Your job comes from the ship category preferences in your character setup, Command, Security, Engineering, Medical, Science, Cargo, Service and Assistant, each set to high, medium or low. Each hull picks its captain first, contested between the players who set Command highest, with ties broken at random; if nobody wants Command, someone is drafted and told so. Everyone else is matched to an open job in a category they asked for, working down from high to low, then to any open job. Job titles vary by hull and theme, so the captain might be called Captain, Team Leader or something stranger. If you join after the round has started, you get a ship menu instead. You can join any existing crew that has an open slot and has left joining enabled, or launch a ship of your own from the shipyard. The two Pill-class hulls are free; everything else costs ship parts you have banked from previous rounds. What is already on your ship Every hull with real rooms launches with the same core kit, wherever the mapper put it. (The two free Pill-class hulls are the exception. They are four tiles, a helm and a cryopod, and nothing else.) Machine What it does Helm console Flies the ship, draws the navigation chart, runs sensor scans, and docks. See Piloting . Mission board and mission pad Take contracts, hand in items on the pad, collect rewards from it. See Missions . Bank machine Your ship's account, which cargo and traders draw on. See Money and Trade . Cargo console Orders supplies against that account. Cryogenic oversight console and cryopods Where latejoiners arrive. Adjusts how many slots each job has, up to six, on a two-minute cooldown. Also where the captain can shut joining off. Autolathe Prints the Research & Development Kit. That last one matters more than it looks. The R&D Kit is a box the autolathe prints for twenty sheets of iron and forty of glass, with no research required, and it contains the R&D console, protolathe, circuit imprinter, destructive analyzer, ship R&D server and the server's source disk. Any ship, however cheap, can build a full research suite on day one. You start with zero research points and no income, so Research is worth reading before someone wastes an hour looking for the machine that generates them. Everything past that core kit comes from your hull's theme and modules: an engine type, a medbay or a chem lab, a mining bay, a galley, a bunkroom. Read Ship Systems for the parts you have to keep running. The loop Fly out, find something worth money, bring it home, spend it, go further out. In practice that means picking a contact off the helm chart and going to look at it. Planets have ore, ruins and fauna; space ruins have loot and usually something guarding it; asteroid fields are the reliable mining stop; trader outposts buy what you dug up and sell what you cannot make. The mission board hands out contracts that point you at all of the above and pays for finishing them. Danger and reward both scale with how close to the star you fly. The safe outer ring is where you start; the deeper rings have better ore yields, nastier wildlife and no rules about shooting each other. The Overmap explains the three zones, and it is the first page you should read after this one. Keeping what you earn Most of what you find is yours only for the round. Ship parts are the exception: they are the persistent currency that unlocks hulls, themes and modules for every future round, and they only carry over if you extract them. To extract, the parts must be inside an extraction case, in your inventory, when the round ends or when your ship makes a bluespace jump out. Use the Request Extraction Case verb in the IC tab to get one. Only the first standard case you are carrying counts, and you have to be alive and conscious, nothing extracts off a corpse. Loose parts in your bag are lost. Everyone who played a character also gets one random part and a hundred credits at round end, so a bad round still moves you forward a little. Staying alive Your ship's hull integrity is not an abstract number. It is literally how much of the ship is still there: every floor tile is worth one point, every wall two, every reinforced wall three. Meteors, missiles and breaches destroy turfs and the integrity drops with them. Below sixty percent the ship starts screaming at you. At fifty percent it stops flying, crash-lands, and becomes a wreck other crews can find and either help or loot. Welding plating back down genuinely repairs it, and a crashed ship that gets rebuilt to sixty-five percent can fly again. A few habits that keep new players breathing: Turn your suit sensors to full before you leave the ship. If you go down on a planet, that is how your crew finds the body. Do not fly into the red ring in your starting hull. Check the zone readout on the helm before you commit to a heading. Take internals for anywhere you have not personally seen the air in. Ruins and unfinished planets are often airless. Repair

title: The Overmap
blurb: The galaxy map your ship flies across. What is out there, how to find it, and why the middle of the map will kill you.
text: The overmap is the galaxy: a 51-by-51 grid of tiles with a star burning at the centre, on which your entire ship is a single icon. Every planet, ruin, trader, storm and rival crew occupies one tile of it. Flying is done from the helm console , and everything you do in a round starts with picking a tile and going there. The single most important thing on this map is not any one destination. It is the three concentric rings of law that decide whether other crews are allowed to shoot you. Moving around Your ship burns its engines in a direction and keeps coasting until you brake, so it handles like a ship and not like a cursor. The helm gives you a heading, a throttle percentage, an engine list and a Stop button that switches between cutting thrust and actively braking. Engines need power and fuel, so a ship that has run dry is a ship that drifts. You can also plot a course: click a charted destination and the autopilot flies there. It routes around known storms, and if it blunders into one anyway it hands control straight back rather than pressing on. Touching the heading controls takes the ship off autopilot silently. Full details are on Piloting . What is out there Contact What it is Planets Landable worlds: lava, ice, jungle, beach and wasteland. Ore, ruins, weather and fauna. See Planets . Space ruins Twelve to twenty-four derelicts, stations and wrecks per round, each a loaded interior with loot and something guarding it. See Ruins . Asteroid storms Landable rock fields, guaranteed at least three per round, and the dependable place to mine in space. Flying through one damages the hull. See Mining . Ion and electrical storms Hazards. Ion storms EMP random parts of your ship. Electrical storms blow out lights and throw lightning around inside the hull, while quietly topping up your power storage. Nebulas Harmless clouds of a specific gas that a ram scoop can harvest, and the only place a ship can hide itself. See Gas Economy . Trader outposts Three permanent markets, one in each ring. They broadcast sector-wide, so they are on your chart from the start. See Trader Outposts . Other ships Player crews and NPC ships , including pirates who will hail you and then interdict you. Dread signals Vestige ruins, which surface one at a time as the round ages, marked in red and named for the patron inside. See Vestige Ruins . Empty space An empty tile can still be docked into, which is how two ships park next to each other. Other things surface on a schedule rather than at roundstart (contested caches, the Grand Colosseum and the lich's lair) and announce themselves on Wideband when they do. Seeing it Two different ranges matter and they are deliberately not the same thing. Sight is a fixed ring of four tiles around your ship. It costs nothing, needs no research, and everything physically inside it draws on the helm chart immediately. Anything you see this way is remembered for the rest of the round, drawn faded once you leave, you chart the sector by flying it. Sensors are an active scan on a one-minute cooldown, and they reach further than you can see. A scan does not reveal things around you; it charts what it finds into your navigation list, where it stays at any distance. It starts at the same four tiles as your sight and grows to six, eight and ten through the radar research tree, which also teaches your sensors to name space ruins instead of listing them as unknown signals, and eventually to identify vessels automatically. Two things escape both. Other ships are never recorded, because they move. An unscanned vessel is an anonymous blip. And storms cannot be scanned at all; the only ways to learn where one is are to fly past it or to buy a star chart from a trader, a one-use slate that charts every contact in one whole ring at once. Traders also sell rumor charts , which name a specific rare ruin and spawn it somewhere uncharted when you decrypt one at the helm. The three zones The map is divided into three static concentric rings measured from the star. They never move and never rotate, so the ring a tile is in is simply how far from the centre it sits. Ring Zone Ship weapons Interdiction and forced docking Outer third (map edge) Neutral Zone Disabled Not allowed Middle third Contested Zone Disabled Allowed Inner third (nearest the star) Lawless Zone Allowed Allowed In plain terms: the outer ring is safe, the middle ring lets someone stop your ship and board it but not shoot it, and the inner ring is open season. The star charts traders sell label the three rings the neutral ring, the contested lanes and the lawless deep. You can always tell which one you are in. The helm names the current zone, describes it, and says outright whether weapons and interdiction are permitted here; the overmap tiles themselves are tinted green, yellow and red. Every player ship spawns in the outer ring at roundstart, so if you have not deliberately flown inward, you are safe. Crossing a boundary is a deliberate act. Thrusting at a tile in a different zone does not move you. It starts a ten-second transition instead, during which your engines are cut and you cannot thrust. The helm announces the zone you are entering and counts down. Pressing Stop cancels it, so you get a free chance to change your mind. The middle ring is not a soft warning Weapons being disabled in the Contested Zone does not make it safe. Anyone can interdict you there, pin you in place and force a dock, and then the fight happens with guns inside your hull. Boarding is the whole point of that ring. Why anyone goes deeper Everything worth having is closer to the star, because the rings scale rewards as well as danger. Rock on planets yields half again as much ore in the Contested Zone and double in the Lawless Zone. Planet wildlife spawns thirty percent denser in yellow and sixty percent denser in red, and each spawn has a twenty or forty percent chance of upgrading to the biome's genuinely dangerous list instead of its ordinary one. title: Piloting Your Ship
blurb: How to fly, scan, and dock your ship from the helm control console.
text: Everything your crew does starts at the helm control console . It flies the ship across the overmap , runs your sensors, and holds the dock controls. Any crew member can use it (it refuses anyone who isn't on the ship's crew) and wall-mounted ship viewscreens show the same display without the controls. Getting underway Press Undock . The console runs a ten-second warmup, then holds a twenty-second lockout before you can undock again. Undocking is blocked while your cargo shuttle is still aboard, and while an enemy interdictor has you locked; below 25% fuel the console asks you to confirm first. Reading the console The panels around the chart are your status board: Panel What it tells you Hull Integrity percent, plus bonus plating. Below 50% the ship is disabled and every helm control stops working. Fuel Average reserve across running engines, then a row per engine with its own level and an on/off switch. Drive Installed thrust, drives online, and whether something is throttling you. Sensors Scan radius, and the buttons that run an active scan. Velocity Speed in tiles per minute, and the time until you cross into the next tile. Heading and position sit in the corner of the chart. The ship's name at the top can be changed by the commanding officer. Flying The compass rose commands a course : eight direction buttons and a square brake in the middle. Press a direction and the ship handles the rest. It sheds any drift working against you, burns up to cruising speed, then cuts the engines and coasts, holding the course on momentum alone. The button stays lit while the course is held, even with the engines cold. Press the lit button to drop the course and coast free. The brake always brakes, whatever the ship is doing; press it again mid-brake to release it. The vertical slider beside the rose is the throttle , 1 to 100 percent. It sets how hard the engines burn and the cruising speed the ship settles at. Full throttle is flat out, half throttle cruises at half speed on a fraction of the fuel. Drag it mid-flight and the ship adjusts on the spot: raising it starts a top-up burn, lowering it sheds the difference for free. A diagonal burn puts half the thrust on each axis, so cutting a corner is not free speed. You can also fly from the keyboard. Click the wasd switch in the corner of the Helm panel to take manual control: while it shows live , WASD or the arrow keys command a course (hold two together for a diagonal), Space brakes, and X cuts the engines to coast, and your character stays put, because the console keeps those keys for itself. The console only holds your keys while its window is the one you are typing at: click into the game world and you walk around as normal, with the switch reading armed until you click back in. Click the switch off or close the console to drop manual control entirely. Nothing stops you automatically Space has no friction. Once the ship reaches cruising speed the engines go cold and it costs nothing to keep going, but keep going it will, forever, until you brake or command something else. Fuel is only ever spent changing your speed, never keeping it. Burning toward a tile in a different zone band starts a zone transition : the engines cut, the ship holds still for ten seconds, then crosses and resumes your course by itself on the far side. The brake cancels the crossing and leaves you where you were. The navigation chart The chart is the middle panel. Drag with the left or middle mouse button to pan, use the wheel or the slider to zoom, and double-click (or press Recentre ) to snap back onto your ship. The coloured rings are the zone bands. Right-click the chart or a contact for the action menu: set a course for the autopilot, interact with something sharing your tile, run a Ships scan on an unknown vessel, or clear a waypoint you are done with. The drawer beside the chart has four tabs. Contacts lists every mark you know about with live distance and bearing. At location lists only things on your tile. The only things you can act on. Comms is the hail log (see Radio & Comms ). Intel holds sealed rumour charts bought from traders, which reveal a rare signal's coordinates when decrypted. Autopilot Right-click a destination and choose Set course . The autopilot flies with the same headings and throttle you would use, so it burns the same fuel and sits out the same zone transitions. It steers, it does not teleport. On a planet, ruin or outpost the same menu offers Travel & dock , which flies there and starts the docking approach the moment it arrives. That includes asteroid fields: a course that ends in a docking approach is allowed to finish on the field itself, so you can send the ship to one and let it dock. Both commands also appear as buttons under the selected contact in the drawer. It routes around storms, asteroid fields and known hostile vessels, but only around things this ship has actually seen . It also prefers space you have charted: tiles nobody aboard has ever looked at cost extra to route through, so a known clean corridor beats a shortcut through the dark, and courses stop wandering off through the unexplored side of the map just because nothing bad is on record there. When it does fly into unexplored tiles it halves cruise speed, so it has time to react to what turns up. The gear button next to the autopilot readout (bottom-left of the chart) opens the flight policy panel, which works whether or not a course is engaged. Changing a setting mid-course re-plans the course immediately under the new rules. Cross asteroid fields / Cross ion storms / Cross EMP clouds — off by default. Switched on, the autopilot treats that kind of weather as a nuisance rather than a wall: it will fly through one when going around costs more, and it tells you at engage time how many such crossings the plotted course contains. With shields up, asteroid impacts are absorbed, which is what makes crossing fields worth switching on. Avoid known hostiles — on by default. Stamps

title: Pirates & NPC Ships
blurb: Seven pirate factions roam the galaxy, scan your bank balance, and call your holopad with a price. What happens if you pay, and what happens if you don't.
text: The galaxy is not empty. Four crewed pirate vessels are active at any one time, drawn from seven factions, spread across the Contested and Lawless bands. They patrol, they hunt, and when they find you they check your bank balance before deciding whether you are worth the trouble. Kill one and a replacement faction moves in to take its place, so the pressure never really goes away. The factions Vessel Who they are Silverscale noble vessel Lizard aristocrats. Methodical, slow to lock, expensive to buy off. Ghostship vessel An undead crew. Relentless boarders, patient negotiators. Toolbox salvage vessel Ex-assistants. A ramshackle ship, terrible engines, and a lot of bodies. Geode crystal vessel Mutated ethereals. Prefer ranged fighting, few boarders. Interdyne biocraft Rogue pharmaceutical researchers looking for "funding". Auditor enforcement vessel The Space IRS. You haven't been paying your taxes. The most expensive demands in the game. Siege warship Medieval warriors who do not understand the engines. Slow, tough, and they love boarding. Faction changes how a fight goes: how fast they get a lock, how often they shoot, how many boarders they throw at you, and how much they ask for. They scan you first A pirate that spots you runs a financial scan before committing. Your ship gets a warning that its financial systems are being scanned. If the scan comes back and you are broke, they disengage. Being poor is a real defence. If you have money, what happens next depends on the zone. In the Contested Zone they cannot shoot you and they will not board. Instead they lock on, pin you with an interdiction field and run a data siphon into your ship account, draining credits for as long as the lock holds. This is a mugging, not a battle. Break the lock and it stops. In the Lawless Zone they hail you first. The hail Your holopads ring. Every pad aboard sounds off, the ship announces an incoming hail, and you have twenty seconds to answer before they open fire. Answer through the holopad interface, the same way you would take an ordinary holo-call. The hostile vessel is listed as an incoming caller. Answering spawns a hologram of the pirate captain on the pad, and they name their price. There is no bartering. You are offered exactly two ways to pay: Credits out of your ship account. The figure is built from a quarter of your balance, adjusted by faction, by how far the fight has already gone (cheapest before combat starts, most expensive to stop one mid-fight) and by how badly damaged they are. A specific item , in a specific quantity. Put them on any mission pad aboard your ship and they get beamed across. Wrong items are refused out loud. You get about two minutes, with impatience warnings at sixty, thirty and ten seconds. Let it run out and the deal is off. Do not fly away mid-negotiation Moving your ship during an active negotiation is read as betrayal. The first time, they interdict you on the spot and raise the demand by half. The second time, they open fire and the negotiation is over. Pay and they disengage, and that ship leaves you alone for five minutes. Refuse, stall out the clock, or get caught fleeing twice, and that ship marks you down permanently. It will not offer you terms again this round. If you refuse Refusal in the Lawless Zone starts a staged assault rather than a straight shootout. About five seconds after the rejection they interdict you, announce the boarding, and roughly thirty seconds later the first pod lands. It runs in three waves with a thirty-second breather between each, the wave sizes scaled to how many crew you had aboard when it started. Between waves the captain taunts you over comms. Repel all three and the enemy commander comes down personally by drop pod. At the same time, if they can, they will shoot: lasers while your shields hold, missiles once they drop, and boarding pods only when your shields are down. The shield wall would swat the pods out of the sky. There is a hard cap of ten hostile boarders aboard your ship at once. Kill the commander and the pirate ship is disabled . It stops fighting, releases its weapons lock and its interdiction, and your ship is told plainly that you may now board and claim it. Boarding them, and taking their ship A pirate ship becomes boardable when it is disabled, when it is interdicted, or when its hull is damaged past three-quarters, and dead in the water counts too, so wrecking their engines works. To actually get across you need an interdiction system of your own: pin them, move onto their overmap tile, and force the dock. Two prizes are on the table. The ship itself. The pirate captain carries a ship authorization key and drops it where they die. Insert that key into the pirate ship's helm console and the vessel becomes yours to fly. If the whole crew is killed and nobody claims it in time, the ship is abandoned and drifts as a derelict. Still claimable, but you were on a clock. The bounty. Every active pirate has a standing bounty listed on your ship's mission board . Bounties are competitive: several crews can accept the same one, and the first to turn in the captain's key gets paid. Yellow-band pirates are worth 5,000 credits, Lawless-band pirates 15,000, and the heavier bounties pay out better loot crates, laser weapons, disablers, armour, batons and security supplies at the low end, premium military gear at the high end. You can also buy tracking on a bounty target, at the cost of a quarter of the reward. You cannot have both. Turning the key in for the bounty spends it; using it to claim the ship fails the bounty. While you are aboard, find their data siphon . Whatever they drained out of your accounts (or somebody else's) is still sitting in it, and interacting with it hands the stored credits back as a holochip. Neutral traffic There isn't any. Every roaming NPC ship in the galaxy is hostile by default, and there is no friendly convoy or merchant traffic to run into. Trade happens at trader outposts , not on the

title: Planets
blurb: The five worlds that appear every round. How to land on one, what will kill you there, and what is worth carrying home.
text: Every round puts five planets on the chart: one volcanic, one frozen, one tropical, one oceanic and one apocalyptic. Each is generated fresh at the start of the round, so nobody can memorise a layout, and each is scaled to the part of the galaxy it sits in. Planets are where ore, wild trade goods, planetary ruins and most of the fauna live, and they are the only places you can walk around outdoors without a hull between you and everything else. Finding one and landing Planets show on the helm chart as coloured contacts, one colour per terrain type, and the contact is already named. A "Frozen Planet" is a frozen planet before anyone scans it. What is on it stays unknown until you land. Fly the ship onto the planet's tile and press Dock; the button reads "(planetfall)". See Piloting for getting there and The Overmap for what the chart is telling you. Two ships can be berthed at a planet at once. If both berths are taken you are told to come back later. If you arrive while the surface is still being built you get "planetary survey in progress", wait a moment and try again. Your ship lands at a fixed berth on the edge of the map unless someone aboard uses an orbital survey console to pick the landing site, which needs research. Drop pods are the other way down. The five worlds Planet Air Storm Notable ground Lava Planet Thin and hot. Bring internals and a suit Ash storm: burns anyone caught outside Basalt, lava flows, tendrils, geysers, telecrystal veins Frozen Planet Breathable but far below freezing Snow storm: cold deep enough to beat your clothing Snow, ice lakes, glacial core veins Tropical Planet Breathable, mild Rain: soaks you, nothing worse Dense jungle, water, wild spice pods Oceanic Planet Breathable, mild Rain: soaks you, nothing worse Beaches, shore water and deep ocean, fishing Apocalyptic Planet Breathable, mild Sandstorm: batters anyone caught outside Dust flats, dead forest, heavy ruins, telecrystal veins Ash storms and sandstorms both roll a harmless variant sometimes, gentle embers or drifting sand instead of the real thing. The real thing announces itself first, and the warning is your cue to get under a roof or back inside the ship. The lava world is not a walk Lava planets have thin air as well as heat, so a gas mask and a tank are not enough on their own. They are also the only planet type where a true megafauna can appear out in the open. At most one per world, but one is plenty. What is down there Rock and ore. Terrain generation carves rock pockets across the surface, and mineral walls sit inside them. This is where most mining happens; see Mining & Salvage . Ruins. Every planet type has its own pool of surface ruins, seeded fresh with the terrain: camps, outposts, wrecks, shrines, laboratories. Frozen, volcanic and apocalyptic worlds have the deepest pools. Ruins carry loot caches and the things guarding them; see Ruins & Points of Interest . Wildlife. Fauna comes from the biome you are standing in. Volcanic ground has goliaths, legions and watchers, and nests that keep producing them. Frozen worlds have wolves, polar bears, snow legions, ice demons and whelps. The apocalyptic world has armed hermits, hivebots, giant spiders and legions in its ruin fields. Jungles have monkeys, gorillas and tarantulas; the ocean world is mostly livestock and butterflies on land and carp in the water. Elite-tier creatures show up as tumours on volcanic and irradiated ground. See Threats & Elites . Tendrils. On volcanic worlds, a corrupted tendril is a permanent nest pouring out monsters. Kill it and the ground around it cracks open. You get about five seconds to grab loot out of the collapse by hand, one crate per person, before the tile becomes a chasm. The crate is worth the fight; see Mining & Salvage . Other worlds have their own nests, but only the volcanic tendril pays out like this. Trade goods. Each world grows or hides something traders want and nobody can manufacture aboard a ship: raw telecrystal in the crust of the volcanic and apocalyptic worlds, glacial cores in frozen permafrost, wild spice pods lying on jungle ground, pearl clams caught in beach shore water. None of them can be scanned for. Telecrystal and glacial veins look like ordinary rock until you swing at them. Prices are at Trader Outposts ; the wider economy is in Money & Trade . Dangerous space means a dangerous planet The five planets are dealt across the galaxy's zone bands, so there is always at least one in the safe ring and at least one out in the lawless deep. A planet's band changes how the same world plays: Fauna spawns thicker, and a share of the rolls upgrade to the biome's meaner list: lone animals become nests. Storms come around more often, give less warning before they hit, and last longer. A planet keeps its band for the whole round. One the crew wrote off as lethal will still be lethal the next time it turns up. Planets do not stay put A planet's surface exists only while someone is using it. Once the last ship undocks and nobody is left alive on the ground, the surface is released about five minutes later. Anything you leave behind is gone with it : dropped gear, stashed loot, a body you meant to come back for, a base you built. Take it with you or lose it. After it releases, the planet reappears somewhere else on the chart, in the same band, as an unvisited contact again. Its terrain is regenerated the next time somebody lands. A crewmate still alive on the surface holds the planet open indefinitely. If someone is stranded, the world will wait for you. Wildlife clears out a few minutes after the last person leaves and repopulates when someone lands again. A planet you are still docked at keeps everything where you left it. Landable asteroid fields Asteroid storms are the other place to put boots on rock. They appear on the chart as hazards in three severities, at least three per round, and you dock inside them at a "mining anchorage". They are not planets (no weather, no ruins, no air) but

title: Player Outposts
blurb: Buying a deed, founding your own station on the overmap, building it out, and defending it from siege.
text: For 10,000 credits and three trade vouchers you can stop renting space and found your own station. A player outpost is a permanent structure on the overmap with its own interior, its own hangar, and a build region you fill in however you like. It lasts the whole round, and where you plant it decides whether anyone is allowed to shoot at it. Buying the deed Outpost deeds are sold over the counter at Waystation Halcyon and Quartermain Depot, on their Colonial Registry shelf. The price is 10,000 credits plus 3 trade vouchers, and it does not go down. A deed is bound to the buyer by name. Nobody else can use it, and each person may hold one active claim per round . If you already founded an outpost this shift, the registry refuses to sell you another deed. Founding To found, your crew's ship has to be holding still on an empty overmap tile , not docked, not moving, and not on top of a planet, ruin or another outpost. Use the deed in hand and the registry catalogue opens. Pick a shell and a name: Shell What you get Compact Habitat One pressurised room with the essential consoles, a hangar elevator, and a charged power bay. Cheap on materials and quick to expand. Waystation Frame A proper station core: separate work and living space, a powered workshop bay, and a hangar elevator off the main hall. More to defend, more room to grow. Bare Claim No prefab at all. An empty sector, a survey pad, and a crate holding the two registry console boards. Bring your own everything, including the floor and the air. Confirming registers the claim, announces it galaxy-wide, and drops the outpost onto the overmap where your ship is sitting. Then fly over and dock to move in. The two prefab shells arrive with lights, a pressurised core, an APC and cable, a charged SMES with an input terminal, and an unanchored portable generator with fuel . The area needs power, so once the SMES buffer drains it is on you to keep the generator fed or build something better. Where you plant it is permanent Zone rules lock in at founding and never change. An outpost founded in the patrolled outer ring is protected from ship weapons forever . An outpost founded in the contested band or the lawless deep is raidable forever . Nothing you build later changes that, and you cannot move it. The consoles Every shell ships with two consoles, and if either is destroyed you can rebuild it, a fresh console relinks itself to whatever outpost's z-level it is standing on. The Bare Claim's starter crate holds both boards. The management console is the owner's control panel. Ownership is tied to your account rather than your body, so it survives death and respawn. Everyone else gets a read-only view. From it you can: Rename the outpost (announced galaxy-wide, on a 5-minute cooldown) and set a public memo. Set the docking policy. Authorise other people to use the construction console. Buy a galaxy-wide broadcast . Transfer ownership to somebody standing on the outpost, or abandon the claim. The construction console puts you behind a remote drone with a built-in RCD, RTD, RPD and RLD, fed from the outpost's ore silo. It is the same tool ships use to expand their hulls, pointed at your claim instead. Anything the drone builds is automatically pulled into the outpost's powered area so it gets light, gravity and APC coverage; anything you build by hand gets swept in the same way within half a minute. You can build anywhere inside the claim's survey bounds , the shell's footprint plus fifteen tiles in every direction. Outside that, nothing. The hangar Both prefab shells arrive with a hangar elevator already installed, which means visiting ships get their own private berth from the moment you found the place, exactly like a trader outpost. Ride the elevator from the concourse to any occupied berth and back. If you took the Bare Claim, or you want the elevator somewhere else, the construction console has a three-step workflow for it: plan projects a coloured blueprint of the elevator kit under your drone, rotate turns it to face another way, and confirm stamps it down and wires it in. Without an elevator, an outpost still has two ordinary landing pads, and that is all. Who is allowed in The management console sets one of three docking policies: Open : anybody may dock without asking. This is the default. By request : a visiting ship's dock attempt queues a request, the owner is notified wherever they are, and they approve or deny it from the console. Approved ships stay approved. Lockdown : only the owner's own crew gets in. You can also ban specific ships outright, which overrides everything including an existing approval. Advertising A broadcast costs 2500 credits off your ID's account and runs for 20 minutes, with a 10-minute cooldown between purchases. Buying one pushes a one-time notification to every crewed ship in the galaxy, lists your outpost with its memo and coordinates on every ship's mission board feed, and pins it on every helm's nav chart for the duration. It is the only way anyone finds a shop, bar or repair yard you have built out in the middle of nowhere. Raiding and siege An outpost founded outside patrolled space is a legitimate military target and shows up on other crews' combat consoles as one. The rules are narrow: only outposts founded outside green space can be locked at all, and a missile launcher will only fire on one while the attacking ship is itself sitting in the contested band or the lawless deep. Nobody shoots at anything from inside patrolled space. Siege damage lands as missiles, and there is no ship-to-ship shield to soak them. What you can build instead is an outpost shield generator . Shield generators The generator is a machine you research (through the shuttle shield systems node), build into a frame, and wrench down inside the claim's survey bounds . While it is anchored, powered and holding charge, incoming missiles detonate at the edge of your survey bounds instead of hitting your buildings. The numbers matter:

title: Research
blurb: Where your ship's research points actually come from, and what the tech tree is worth spending them on.
text: Research in Voidcrew is per-ship . Your crew's tech tree lives on a hard drive in your own R&D server, it starts completely empty, and nothing you unlock is shared with any other crew. It is also the only route to things no trader stocks: longer sensor range and transporters. This page covers where the points come from and where they are worth spending. The suite Almost every hull carries an autolathe, and that one machine is enough. Print the Research & Development Kit (twenty sheets of iron and forty of glass, no research required) and the box holds the boards for the whole chain: R&D console, protolathe, destructive analyzer, circuit imprinter, ship R&D server, and the source code disk that goes in the server. See Ship Systems for where these sit aboard. The disk is the techweb. Slot it into the server and that server hosts your research; pull it out and the research goes with it. The autolathe prints a spare disk for two sheets of glass, but a fresh disk is a fresh blank tree, not a copy. Everything that earns or spends points has to be told which server it belongs to. Slotting the source disk into the server claims every scanner and operating computer aboard that has no link yet , so build the server whenever you like and anything you made earlier falls in behind it. Everything else, R&D console, orbital survey console, protolathe, nanite chamber, destructive scanner. Is linked by hand: multitool the server, then the machine. One click, including to move a machine from one server to another. A scanner with no server says so when you examine it and buzzes when you try to use it, so an unlinked machine is obvious rather than silently useless. Copy your research before you risk it An R&D console with a technology disk in it can download everything you have researched. That disk uploads into any other ship's console, so a second copy is cheap insurance and a fair trade good. The console refuses to download for anyone who is not on the ship's crew. Earning points Ships launch with no research income at all . No hull is mapped with a survey scanner or an orbital survey console, and an R&D server generates nothing by sitting there powered. Every point below is something a crew member goes and does. Sources are listed roughly in the order a new crew can reach them. Source Pays What it needs Experiments 2,000 each An Experi-Scanner, which you can print from the start Research notes found as loot 250 – 10,000 per document Getting off the ship Orbital survey console 50 – 1,000 per contact, plus the same in credits One 40-point research node Survey scanner 50 – 200 per two-second cycle, multiplied by its parts A 1,000-point node, and a lot of power Anomaly cores in the destructive analyzer 200 per core type, nine types The anomaly refinery chain Dissection 10 per body, up to 2,000 with the full ladder Nothing to start Robbing another ship's server 2,500 per attempt Boarding somebody Experiments: the best thing you can do in the first ten minutes This is the strongest early faucet in the game and it costs nothing. Every completed experiment pays a flat 2,000 points . The Experi-Scanner is a protolathe design your web already has at round start, and it prints for half a sheet each of iron and glass. It finds your server on its own; check the examine text, and multitool it across if it says it has no link. Use it in your hand to pick an experiment, then hit whatever the experiment wants with it. Your R&D console's experiment panel shows everything currently on offer with a progress bar and a hint. A blank techweb already carries several, including: Scan three patches of blood or vomit. That is the whole experiment. Scan three different species of fish. A basic fishing rod is also a free design. Scan a beaker of a named chemical at high purity. Autopsy a corpse on an operating table wired to your server. That one is done with an autopsy scanner , which cannot be printed: order the Autopsy Kit crate from your cargo console . More experiments appear as you research deeper into a branch, so the supply does not dry up. The fishing chain pays a small bonus on top of the flat 2,000. Ordnance experiments pay the same 2,000, but they are finished differently: you capture a tank explosion on a doppler array or burst a gas tank in a tank compressor, print the data to a disk, and publish it through the NT Frontier app. Nine of them exist (five explosive and four gas) and each pays the first time a paper actually completes it. Publishing further tiers of an experiment you have already finished pays nothing. Research notes Research notes are a physical document with a point value printed on it. Put one against a linked R&D console and the points go straight into your web. Hit one note with another to stack them into a single bigger document. They turn up as loot, and the good ones are worth a lot: documents found in the wild are worth 250, 1,000, 2,500, 5,000 or 10,000 points. Research-themed loot caches carry one at every zone tier, cave dens on wasteland planets and old barrels on beach planets both roll the 5,000 and 10,000 tiers, and space ruins sometimes have one lying on a desk. This is the fastest way to a big number, and it is a good reason to have someone on every landing party checking the paperwork. Salvaged documents can also be sold through the cargo console at half a credit per point, if your crew would rather have money than tech. The orbital survey console The Orbital survey console costs a single 40-point node, which makes it the first thing most crews research. It surveys whatever your ship is sharing an overmap tile with. You sit in orbit alongside it, you do not have to dock. A survey takes 60 seconds and is cancelled the moment the ship moves, so park first. It pays points and an identical amount in credits, both banked in the console: Print research turns the points into a research-notes document, and Cash out spits the credits out as physical bills.
